# Overview

**qmd-fast** is a single-purpose Rust dev server that renders `.qmd` files to
HTML (blog posts, reveal.js slides, books) for one author's writing workflow. It
is not a general Quarto replacement. The whole tool is organised around three
load-bearing goals:

- **Click-to-source.** Every rendered block knows exactly where it came from, so
  you can jump from the preview back to the line that produced it.
- **Block-level incremental updates.** Saving a file re-renders only the blocks
  that changed, leaving everything else (including live canvases) untouched.
- **No per-edit startup cost.** A warm server and a warm Jupyter kernel mean
  edits are reflected immediately, with no cold start on every save.

::: {.callout-note}
## Scope

qmd-fast renders to HTML only. There is no PDF path and no format matrix. The
"spec" is a small corpus of real documents under `corpus/`: when those render
correctly, the tool is done.
:::

This page is itself a `.qmd` rendered by qmd-fast, so the
[Feature showcase](#feature-showcase) below is *live*, not a description. Run it
with `serve docs/index.qmd 4321` to see the interactive examples execute.

# Quick start

Start the live preview server and edit with instant updates:

```sh
cargo run -p qmd-fast-server -- preview post.qmd 4321   # aliases: dev, serve
```

Then open `http://127.0.0.1:4321`. Save the file and watch only the edited block
update in place, with scroll position preserved. Add `--host` to expose it on
your network with a QR code and open the same *live* preview on a phone (see
[Reading on any screen](#reading-on-any-screen)).

To produce output instead of previewing, `build` writes a self-contained HTML
file (or, with `--out <dir>`, a portable folder with copied assets) and `render`
streams a page to stdout:

```sh
cargo run -p qmd-fast-server -- build  post.qmd             # post.html beside the source
cargo run -p qmd-fast-server -- build  post.qmd --out dist  # dist/index.html + copied assets
cargo run -p qmd-fast-server -- render post.qmd > out.html  # one-shot page to stdout
```

A `~/.local/bin/qmd-fast` launcher on `PATH` (it rebuilds the release binary when
the tool's sources change) lets you drop the prefix: `qmd-fast preview post.qmd`.

# Architecture

All of the intelligence lives in the Rust core behind a stable websocket
protocol. The browser preview is a thin client, as @fig-architecture shows.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-architecture
%%| fig-cap: "qmd-fast architecture: thin clients talk to the server over a websocket, and all rendering lives in the Rust core."
flowchart LR
  BR["Browser preview<br/>(vanilla JS)"]
  subgraph Server["qmd-fast server"]
    direction TB
    WS["Websocket<br/>+ file watcher"]
    subgraph Core["qmd-fast-core"]
      direction TB
      P["Parser<br/>comrak + sourcepos"] --> M["Block model<br/>+ diff"] --> R["Render<br/>html / reveal / book"]
    end
    K["Warm Jupyter kernel"]
  end
  F[(".qmd files")]
  BR <-->|JSON protocol| WS
  WS --> P
  R -->|changed blocks| WS
  F -.->|watch| WS
  M -->|code cells| K --> M
```

| Component | Crate / path | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| Core | `crates/core` | Parsing (comrak + sourcepos), the block model, HTML rendering |
| Server | `crates/server` | Websocket dev server, file watcher, Jupyter kernel pool |
| Web client | `web-client/` | Browser preview client (vanilla JS) — the client |

The protocol is open, so an embedded editor client (a VS Code extension, etc.) is
a new thin client, not a rewrite. A save flows through the pipeline as
@fig-save-flow shows:

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-save-flow
%%| fig-cap: "How a save flows through the pipeline: only the changed blocks are pushed to the preview."
flowchart LR
  save["Save .qmd"] --> watch["File watcher"]
  watch --> parse["Re-parse + block model"]
  parse --> diff["Diff by block id"]
  diff --> ws["Websocket:<br/>changed blocks only"]
  ws --> dom["Preview updates<br/>in place"]
```

# The block model

Every top-level element is a **block**. Each block carries three data
attributes that the rest of the system keys off:

- `data-block-id` is a content hash (with a positional tiebreak for duplicates).
  Because it is content-derived, an unchanged block keeps its id across edits and
  is never touched.
- `data-sourcepos` is the `startLine:startCol-endLine:endCol` range the block
  came from. This is what powers click-to-source in both directions.
- `data-source-file` is present only on blocks pulled in from an
  `{{< include >}}`d file, so cross-file source mapping still works.

Source mapping, incremental re-render, and live-state preservation all build on
this one model.

# The websocket protocol

On connect, the server sends a `full_render`; on each save it diffs the new block
list against the old one and broadcasts only the differences.

| Direction | Message | Payload |
|---|---|---|
| server to client | `full_render` | `title`, `body_html`, `diagnostics` |
| server to client | `update` | `target_id`, `html` |
| server to client | `insert` | `after_id`, `html` |
| server to client | `remove` | `target_id` |
| server to client | `diagnostics` | `messages` (non-fatal include / kernel issues) |
| server to client | `error` | `message` (a failed render; shown as an overlay) |
| client to server | `click_block` | `block_id`, `source_file`, `sourcepos` |

Double-clicking a block opens its source in your editor — a
`vscode://file/…:line:col` deep link by default (so it assumes VS Code for now).
The client also speaks a `postMessage` protocol as the integration surface for an
embedded editor client: it posts `qmd-goto` up to a host (which reveals the
source) and accepts `qmd-cursor` to highlight the block under the editor cursor.

# Feature showcase

Everything below is produced from this page's own `.qmd` source. The interactive
Observable examples need a running server (the runtime does not work over
`file://`), and the executable Python examples additionally need a kernel (see
[Code execution](#code-execution)); with `serve` they are fully live.

## Prose and typography

Standard Markdown works as expected: **bold**, *italic*, ~~strikethrough~~,
`inline code`, [links](https://example.com), nested lists, blockquotes, and pipe
tables with per-column alignment:

| Capability | Status | Where |
|:--|:--:|--:|
| Block model + diff | ✅ | `crates/core` |
| Live Observable cells | ✅ | vendored runtime |
| PDF / non-HTML output | ❌ | out of scope |

> Smart typography turns straight quotes into curly ones and handles ellipses…,
> matching the look of the author's existing posts.

Code blocks are syntax-highlighted **server-side** (in Rust, via syntect) and get
a hover **Copy** button. Like the math, highlighting ships fully offline: the
colors are emitted as scope classes the theme styles, so the exported HTML needs
no CDN, the first paint is already colored, and the light/dark toggle restyles
code with nothing to re-run on the client.

```rust
/// Every rendered block carries a content-hash id and its source range.
struct Block {
    id: String,        // stable across edits while the content is unchanged
    sourcepos: String, // "startLine:startCol-endLine:endCol"
    html: String,
}
```

## Math

Math renders server-side with KaTeX and ships fully offline (the fonts are inlined
at build time). Inline math like $e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0$ sits in running text; display
math stands alone; and a labelled equation is **numbered and cross-referencable**.
The discrete Fourier transform [@cooley1965] is given by @eq-dft:

$$
X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n]\, e^{-2\pi i k n / N}
$$ {#eq-dft}

Multi-line aligned environments work too:

$$
\begin{aligned}
  \nabla \cdot \mathbf{E} &= \rho/\varepsilon_0 \\
  \nabla \times \mathbf{B} &= \mu_0\mathbf{J} + \mu_0\varepsilon_0 \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Live interactive content (Observable / OJS)

`{ojs}` cells execute client-side against a vendored Observable runtime: reactive
cells, `viewof` inputs, `Plot`, and `d3` all work, and a cell re-runs automatically
when an input it depends on changes. Drag the slider to add odd harmonics to a
square-wave Fourier synthesis and watch the curve sharpen:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof harmonics = Inputs.range([1, 12], {value: 3, step: 1, label: "Harmonics"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.lineY(
  Array.from({length: 500}, (_, t) =>
    d3.range(1, harmonics + 1).reduce(
      (sum, k) => sum + Math.sin(2 * Math.PI * (2 * k - 1) * t / 500) / (2 * k - 1), 0)),
  {curve: "basis", stroke: "#4c8dff"}
).plot({height: 200, marginLeft: 36, y: {label: "amplitude"}})
```

### The Python → OJS bridge

`ojs_define()` in a Python cell hands values to OJS, so you can compute in Python
and render reactively in the browser. (This part needs a kernel.)

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Python: sample a noisy sine wave"
import math, random
random.seed(7)
signal = [math.sin(2 * math.pi * i / 40) + random.uniform(-0.3, 0.3) for i in range(120)]
ojs_define(signal=signal)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  height: 180, marginLeft: 36,
  marks: [Plot.ruleY([0]), Plot.lineY(signal, {stroke: "#2bb673"})]
})
```

### 3D graphics (Three.js / WebGL)

Because OJS cells can `import` any ES module, **3D visualizations work too**. This
cell pulls Three.js and `OrbitControls` from a CDN, wraps an equirectangular world
map onto a sphere, and returns the live `<canvas>`. Drag to spin the globe yourself
(it also auto-rotates), the **⛶** button takes it fullscreen via the native
Fullscreen API (resizing the renderer to fill the screen), and the renderer is
transparent (`alpha`), so the globe sits straight on the page background and
follows the light/dark theme.
`invalidation` stops the animation loop when the block re-renders. The author's PCA
post drives interactive WebGL point clouds the same way: Python computes the data,
`ojs_define` hands it to a Three.js scene.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const THREE = await import("https://esm.sh/three@0.163.0");
  const { OrbitControls } = await import(
    "https://esm.sh/three@0.163.0/examples/jsm/controls/OrbitControls"
  );

  const w = 600, h = 360;
  const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ antialias: true, alpha: true });
  renderer.setPixelRatio(Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio, 2));
  renderer.setSize(w, h, false); // buffer only; CSS below drives the displayed size
  renderer.setClearColor(0x000000, 0); // transparent: shows the page bg / theme
  // Drive the display size from CSS so the canvas keeps its 600x360 aspect when the
  // page width clamps it (mobile): the width shrinks and the height follows, instead
  // of the fixed inline height squishing it sideways.
  const cv = renderer.domElement;
  cv.style.cssText = `display:block;width:${w}px;max-width:100%;height:auto`;

  const scene = new THREE.Scene();
  const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(40, w / h, 0.1, 100);
  camera.position.set(0, 0, 4);
  scene.add(new THREE.AmbientLight(0xffffff, 1.7));
  const key = new THREE.DirectionalLight(0xffffff, 0.6);
  key.position.set(5, 3, 5);
  scene.add(key);

  const globe = new THREE.Mesh(
    new THREE.SphereGeometry(1.3, 64, 64),
    new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ roughness: 1, metalness: 0 })
  );
  scene.add(globe);

  // Equirectangular world map onto the sphere. If it can't load (e.g. offline),
  // fall back to a drawn lat/long graticule so the globe is never blank.
  function graticule() {
    const c = document.createElement("canvas");
    c.width = 1024; c.height = 512;
    const x = c.getContext("2d");
    x.fillStyle = "#1f3a5f"; x.fillRect(0, 0, c.width, c.height);
    x.strokeStyle = "rgba(255,255,255,0.35)"; x.lineWidth = 2;
    for (let lon = 0; lon <= c.width; lon += c.width / 24) {
      x.beginPath(); x.moveTo(lon, 0); x.lineTo(lon, c.height); x.stroke();
    }
    for (let lat = 0; lat <= c.height; lat += c.height / 12) {
      x.beginPath(); x.moveTo(0, lat); x.lineTo(c.width, lat); x.stroke();
    }
    return new THREE.CanvasTexture(c);
  }
  new THREE.TextureLoader().load(
    "https://unpkg.com/three-globe/example/img/earth-day.jpg",
    (tex) => {
      tex.colorSpace = THREE.SRGBColorSpace;
      globe.material.map = tex;
      globe.material.emissiveMap = tex;            // lift the unlit side so it reads in light mode
      globe.material.emissive = new THREE.Color(0xffffff);
      globe.material.emissiveIntensity = 0.3;
      globe.material.needsUpdate = true;
    },
    undefined,
    () => { globe.material.map = graticule(); globe.material.needsUpdate = true; }
  );

  const ctrl = new OrbitControls(camera, renderer.domElement);
  ctrl.enableDamping = true;
  ctrl.dampingFactor = 0.06;
  ctrl.enablePan = false;
  ctrl.minDistance = 2;
  ctrl.maxDistance = 8;
  ctrl.autoRotate = true;
  ctrl.autoRotateSpeed = 0.6;

  let raf;
  (function animate() {
    raf = requestAnimationFrame(animate);
    ctrl.update();
    renderer.render(scene, camera);
  })();

  // Wrap the canvas so a fullscreen button can overlay it. Native fullscreen
  // (not the figure lightbox, which clones nodes and would kill a live WebGL
  // canvas) resizes the renderer to fill the screen on fullscreenchange.
  const box = document.createElement("div");
  box.style.cssText = "position:relative;display:inline-block;max-width:100%";
  box.appendChild(renderer.domElement);

  const fsBtn = document.createElement("button");
  fsBtn.textContent = "⛶ Fullscreen";
  fsBtn.style.cssText =
    "position:absolute;bottom:8px;right:8px;padding:4px 10px;font-size:12px;cursor:pointer;" +
    "background:rgba(30,30,30,.75);color:#ddd;border:1px solid #555;border-radius:4px;backdrop-filter:blur(4px)";
  fsBtn.onclick = () =>
    document.fullscreenElement ? document.exitFullscreen() : box.requestFullscreen();
  box.appendChild(fsBtn);

  function onFS() {
    const fs = document.fullscreenElement === box;
    if (fs) {
      // Fill the screen and let the canvas drive off the box's *measured* size: the
      // inline max-width:100% would otherwise cap the box and the camera aspect
      // (screen.* used to be wrong here) wouldn't match the displayed canvas, which
      // stretched the globe. Measure after forcing the fill so the two always agree.
      box.style.maxWidth = "none"; box.style.width = "100vw"; box.style.height = "100vh";
      cv.style.cssText = "display:block;width:100%;height:100%";
      const fw = box.clientWidth, fh = box.clientHeight;
      renderer.setSize(fw, fh, false);
      camera.aspect = fw / fh;
    } else {
      box.style.maxWidth = "100%"; box.style.width = ""; box.style.height = "";
      renderer.setSize(w, h, false);
      camera.aspect = w / h;
      cv.style.cssText = `display:block;width:${w}px;max-width:100%;height:auto`;
    }
    camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
    // Native fullscreen paints a black backdrop; fill it with the page background
    // (--qmd-bg) so it follows the theme, and go transparent again when inline.
    const cs = getComputedStyle(document.documentElement);
    box.style.background = fs
      ? (cs.getPropertyValue("--qmd-bg").trim() || getComputedStyle(document.body).backgroundColor)
      : "";
    fsBtn.textContent = fs ? "✕ Exit fullscreen" : "⛶ Fullscreen";
  }
  document.addEventListener("fullscreenchange", onFS);

  invalidation.then(() => {
    cancelAnimationFrame(raf); ctrl.dispose(); renderer.dispose();
    document.removeEventListener("fullscreenchange", onFS);
  });

  return box;
}
```

## Code execution

A fenced cell tagged with a language runs against a warm Jupyter kernel; its
outputs become their own blocks tied to the cell's id:

```{python}
#| echo: true
import numpy as np
np.arange(5).sum()
```

On save, only cells whose source changed (plus downstream cells) re-execute, and
the kernel never cold-starts. Point the server at a Python with `ipykernel` via
the `QMD_FAST_PYTHON` environment variable; without one, a cell renders as
highlighted source rather than failing.

### Folded code

`#| code-fold: true` collapses a listing behind a summary (label it with
`code-summary`), so long setup code stays out of the way until clicked:

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the setup"
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
draws = rng.normal(size=10_000)
round(float(draws.mean()), 3), round(float(draws.std()), 3)
```

## Raw HTML passthrough

A `{=html}` block is emitted verbatim, so you can drop in markup the Markdown
grammar doesn't cover (custom widgets, embeds, audio players):

```{=html}
<div style="display:flex;gap:.6rem;align-items:center;padding:.7rem 1rem;border-radius:10px;
            color:var(--qmd-fg);border:1px solid var(--qmd-border);
            background:linear-gradient(90deg,rgba(99,102,241,.16),rgba(236,72,153,.16));
            font:600 14px ui-sans-serif,system-ui">
  <span style="font-size:1.5rem">🔌</span>
  <span>This badge is raw HTML, passed through by a <code>{=html}</code> block, not escaped. Its
        inline styles use the page's theme variables, so it tracks light/dark too.</span>
</div>
```

## Figures, captions, and lightbox

A standalone image with a `{#fig-…}` attribute, or a code cell tagged with
`#| label: fig-…` and `#| fig-cap:`, becomes a numbered `<figure>`; clicking it
opens a full-screen lightbox, and `@fig-` cross-references resolve to its number.
@fig-scree is drawn by a matplotlib cell that sets *no* theme colours: inline
figures default to a transparent background with neutral-grey axes, ticks, and
labels, so they track the light/dark theme on their own and only the data colours
are the author's. As it shows, the variance drops off after the third component:

```{python}
#| label: fig-scree
#| fig-cap: "Variance explained per principal component. Click to zoom."
#| echo: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

components = range(1, 8)
explained = [42, 26, 15, 8.5, 5, 2.5, 1]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.4), tight_layout=True)
ax.bar(components, explained, width=0.6, color="#4c8dff", alpha=0.85)
ax.plot(
    components, explained,
    color="#e0566b", linewidth=2, linestyle="--", marker="o", markersize=4,
)
ax.annotate(
    "elbow", xy=(3, 15), xytext=(3.6, 27),
    color="#e0566b", fontsize=11,
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#e0566b"),
)
ax.set_xlabel("Principal component")
ax.set_ylabel("Variance explained (%)")
ax.set_xticks(list(components))
for spine in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

## The full block model (click to expand)

Every top-level element carries `data-block-id` (a content hash), `data-sourcepos`
(its source range), and, for included files, `data-source-file`. Source mapping,
incremental re-render, and live-state preservation all build on this one model.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
Unterminated or empty divs degrade gracefully rather than breaking the page.
:::

## Diagrams

A `{mermaid}` code block renders client-side with mermaid.js, loaded lazily the
first time a diagram appears. The flowcharts in [Architecture](#architecture)
above are rendered exactly this way, and like figures they are **click-to-zoom**:
click a diagram to open it full-screen in the lightbox.

Adding `%%| label: fig-…` and `%%| fig-cap:` turns a diagram into a **numbered,
captioned figure** you can cross-reference, just like an image. As @fig-render
shows, the three output kinds share one pipeline:

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-render
%%| fig-cap: "One block model, three render targets."
flowchart LR
  Q[".qmd"] --> BM["block model"]
  BM --> H["HTML page"]
  BM --> R["reveal.js deck"]
  BM --> K["book + TOC"]
```

## Citations and cross-references

With a `bibliography:` in the front matter, `[@key]` citations become numbered
links to an auto-generated References section, formatted from the BibTeX file.
This page cites the *TeXbook* [@knuth1984] and the FFT paper [@cooley1965], and
groups with locators work too: [@knuth1984; @cooley1965, p. 297]. Cross-references
resolve to labelled links across `@fig-`, `@sec-`, `@tbl-`, `@eq-`, `@lst-`,
`@thm-`, and `@def-`, carrying the resolved number when known (as `@eq-dft` and
`@fig-scree` above do).

## Reveal.js slides

A deck is just a different front-matter `format: revealjs`. Headings split the
document into slides, a title slide is generated from the metadata, and block-swap
still works within the current slide so live edits never reset your position.
[`docs/tour.qmd`](tour.qmd) is a runnable example: `serve docs/tour.qmd 4321`.

## Books and a live table of contents

A document with `toc: true` gains a table of contents built from its heading
anchors and rebuilt live as you edit, with the current section highlighted as you
scroll (a scrollspy). On a wide screen it's a sticky sidebar; on a phone it
collapses into a pull-up sheet (see
[Reading on any screen](#reading-on-any-screen)). This very page is the demo: the
contents beside the text are generated from these headings.

## Multi-page websites

Point either command at a **directory** (instead of a single `.qmd`) and qmd-fast
treats it as a website project. The directory needs one root config, `_quarto.yml`
(Quarto-compatible), which names the site title, the navbar, and the footer; every
`.qmd` under it (skipping `_`-prefixed partials) becomes a page.

```sh
qmd-fast build   corpus/tech-blog            # static site -> _site/ (deployable)
qmd-fast preview corpus/tech-blog            # live site on http://127.0.0.1:4321
```

`build` writes one `.html` per page (mirroring the input tree) and copies the
referenced assets, so the output folder deploys as-is. `preview` serves the same
site **live**: the navbar and post prev/next links navigate between pages (each a
real page load with its own websocket), and the page you are editing hot-reloads
in place with the usual block diff. Intra-site `.qmd` links (including
`other-page.qmd#anchor`) are rewritten to their `.html` targets automatically.

Config is **two levels, no cascade**: the root `_quarto.yml` sets project-wide
defaults and a page's own front matter overrides them. There is deliberately no
Quarto-style `_metadata.yml` directory merge, the single most confusing part of
its model. The chrome is a leaner take on Quarto's website: a theme-aware sticky
navbar (with the theme and click-to-source toggles folded in, and a no-JS mobile
menu), a slim footer, and restyled prev/next, all driven by the same `--qmd-*`
variables a theme extension already styles. There is no title banner, no bundled
search, and no RSS feed.

A `listing:` block turns a page into an index: it crawls the `contents:` directory
and emits a card per document (image, date, title, description, categories), sorted
by `date` and capped by `max-items`. `type: grid` lays them out as a card grid
(collapsing to one column on a phone); the default is a stacked list. With
`listing: { id: x }` the cards fill a `::: {#x}` block (e.g. a homepage "recent
posts" section); otherwise they're appended to the page. So the blog index, the
projects index, and the homepage's recent-posts all generate from front matter.

An `about:` block turns a page into a profile: it renders a centered header (a
round image, the page title as the name, and any `links:`) in place of the normal
title block. The `template:` (jolla, trestles, …) is kept as a styling hook; the
shipped layout is the centered jolla style.

## Reading on any screen

The reading layout is responsive, so the same document works on a laptop and a
phone. Wide tables, long code, display math, and embedded canvases scroll within
their own box instead of stretching the page, type and spacing tighten on narrow
screens, in-page links scroll smoothly, and everything honours
`prefers-reduced-motion`.

On a phone the table of contents becomes a **pull-up sheet**: a quiet handle at
the bottom edge that you drag up (or tap) to open the contents, with the current
section flashing in as you scroll. It is keyboard- and screen-reader-friendly,
Enter/Space to open, Escape to close, and focus moves into the sheet.

To see it on a real device, start the server with `--host`:

```sh
cargo run -p qmd-fast-server -- preview docs/index.qmd --host
```

That binds your LAN, prints a `network` URL, and renders a QR code in the
terminal. Scan it and the *live* preview opens on your phone, updating as you edit
on your laptop.

Pressing **Cmd/Ctrl-P** gives a clean print/PDF: the control bar, TOC handle, and
diagnostics are hidden, the palette forces light, and content flows full width
without clipping code, tables, or math.

## Themes

`theme:` selects the built-in `light` (default) or `dark`, a `.css`/`.scss` file,
or an installed `_extensions/<name>/` bundle. See [THEMING.md](THEMING.md) for
authoring one; a theme is just a `:root` block of CSS custom properties.

## Click-to-source and editor sync

In the browser preview, single-clicking a block highlights it (and reports it to
the server); double-clicking opens its exact source line in your editor (including
across `{{< include >}}`d files) via a `vscode://` deep link — VS Code is assumed
for now. The client still speaks the `qmd-goto`/`qmd-cursor` `postMessage`
protocol, so an embedded editor client can host the preview and add reverse cursor
sync without forking it.

## Live-edit feedback

The edit loop surfaces what is happening without you watching the terminal:

- The block you just changed **pulses** briefly when it re-renders, so your eye
  (or your phone) lands on the edit.
- The control bar shows a live **word count and reading time** for the prose.
- A non-fatal problem (a broken `{{< include >}}`, a missing kernel) appears as a
  small **diagnostics** note in the corner; a *failed* render throws a prominent,
  dismissible **error overlay** over the last good content, so a broken save is
  impossible to miss. It clears on the next successful render.
- The watcher follows the whole document, not just the served file: editing an
  included subsection, the `.bib`, or theme CSS refreshes the preview too.

# CLI reference

| Command | Effect |
|---|---|
| `preview <file.qmd> [port]` | Live preview server (default port 4321; aliases `dev`, `serve`) |
| `preview <file.qmd> --host` | …also exposed on your LAN with a QR code for phones |
| `preview <dir>` | Live **multi-page site** preview (cross-page nav + per-page hot reload) |
| `build <file.qmd> [out.html]` | Write a self-contained HTML file (default `<name>.html`) |
| `build <file.qmd> --out <dir>` | Write `<dir>/index.html` + copied assets (a portable folder) |
| `build <dir> [--out <dir>]` | Build a **multi-page site** to `_site/` (one `.html` per page + assets) |
| `render <file.qmd>` | Render a one-shot full HTML page to stdout |
| `blocks <file.qmd>` | List block ids and sourcepos (for debugging) |

A `qmd-fast` launcher on `PATH` (`~/.local/bin/qmd-fast`) rebuilds the release
binary when the tool's sources change, then runs it, so `qmd-fast preview <file>`
works from anywhere. `--open` launches a browser; `QMD_FAST_PYTHON` points the
server at a Python with `ipykernel` for code execution.
